item.research_question: Can large tensile ductility be achieved at high-stress levels in metallic nanopillars, and what are the underlying deformation mechanisms enabling room-temperature super-elongation in high-entropy alloys?
item.material_system: Single-crystalline <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanopillars; also compared with pure Al, Ni, Ag, Al0.1CoCrFeNi, and CoCrNi nanopillars
item.processing_route: Bulk CoCrFeNi fabricated by arc melting equiatomic pure metal powders (>99.9% purity), homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h, cold rolled (65% reduction), and annealed at 1373 K for 1 h; nanopillars with ~350 nm length and ~70 nm width fabricated via focused ion beam (FIB) milling using 30 kV/300 pA and 50 pA beams, with final cleaning at 5 kV/100 pA; in situ tensile testing performed at room temperature with a strain rate of ~2.8 × 10−3 s−1
item.test_conditions: Room temperature; uniaxial tensile loading along <100>, <110>, and <111> crystallographic directions; strain rate of ~2.8 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM and STEM characterization; large-scale molecular dynamics simulations at 300 K with strain rate of 5 × 108 s−1
key_findings: Achieved uniform tensile elongation of ~110% at flow stresses of 0.6–1.0 GPa in <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi nanopillars at room temperature.
The <100> and <111> oriented nanopillars exhibited very limited plasticity due to shear localization and deformation twinning, respectively.
Deformation was mediated by spatial and synergistic coordination of deformation twinning and dislocation slip, with twin fraction reaching ~90% in simulations.
Nanoscale twins with an average thickness of ~1 nm nucleated, propagated, interacted, and coalesced, leading to lattice reorientation from <110> to <100>.
Detwinning and twin thickening occurred via partial dislocation emission from twin boundary (TB) and free surface intersections.
Generalized stacking fault energy (SFE) in CoCrFeNi showed substantial scattering (wide distribution) due to atomic-level compositional heterogeneities, unlike the fixed SFE in pure Ni.
Pure metal nanopillars (Al, Ni, Ag) showed lower elongation (~30% for Al/Ni, ~60% for Ag) with premature failure due to hindered twin propagation.
Critical twinning stress calculated to be 628–903 MPa, consistent with experimental yield strength range of 0.6–1.0 GPa.
item.mechanism: The ultrahigh uniform tensile ductility arises from the spatial and synergistic activation of deformation twinning and dislocation slip, driven by atomic-level chemical compositional heterogeneities that create a wide spectrum of local stacking fault energies. This variability allows for persistent nucleation of partial dislocations and continuous twin propagation/coalescence, which delocalize plastic strain, suppress strain localization, and delay necking failure.
item.limitations: The study notes that initial dislocation density and width-thickness ratio significantly influence dislocation density evolution but have weak influence on twin fraction evolution; the authors state that quantifying these influences further is needed. Additionally, the simulations used a high strain rate (5 × 108 s−1) compared to experiments, and the effect of short-range ordering (SRO) was found to slightly increase yield strength but not fundamentally alter the deformation mechanism.
item.future_work: The authors state: 'In the future, we will further quantify the influences of initial dislocation density, width-thickness ratio, and other configuration parameters (including sample shape/morphology and atomic ordering) on the evolutions of dislocation density and twin fraction, which is crucial for understanding the plastic deformation behaviors and mechanisms of HEAs.'
quotes: unusual room-temperature uniform elongation up to ~110% at a high flow stress of 0.6–1.0 GPa
spatial and synergistic coordination of deformation twinning and dislocation slip, which effectively promote deformation delocalization and delay necking failure
